title: Seizures & Status Epilepticus: Recognition, Rescue & Safety
html:
A seizure is a transient episode of abnormal brain electrical activity; it may present as staring, altered responsiveness, unusual sensory or motor behavior, or bilateral convulsions. Epilepsy is a longer-term diagnosis and should not be assigned from a single event by the RN. The practical bedside questions are: Is the patient safe and breathing? How long has the episode lasted? Is consciousness returning? Is there a reversible cause? A generalized convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery needs immediate emergency treatment for possible status epilepticus.

Learning goals

  • Describe seizure observations accurately without assuming all events are generalized convulsions.
  • Use safe seizure first aid and identify when to activate emergency rescue.
  • Support ordered benzodiazepine-first treatment and further therapy for ongoing convulsive status epilepticus.
  • Recognize possible nonconvulsive seizures when responsiveness does not return.
  • Assess causes, medication safety, recovery, and an individualized seizure action plan.

Recognize and document the event

Current ILAE classification uses focal, generalized, unknown whether focal or generalized, and unclassified main seizure categories. A focal seizure may begin with one-sided movement, an unusual sensation, speech arrest, or behavior change; it can occur with preserved or impaired consciousness and may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. A generalized seizure may involve tonic-clonic movements or other manifestations. Do not infer the origin solely from the most dramatic movement. Ask witnesses what happened first, then document onset time, sequence, eyes and gaze, head turn, side and type of movement, responsiveness, breathing and color, injuries, incontinence if present, end time, and the recovery pattern. Tongue biting or incontinence may support a diagnosis but is neither required nor sufficient.

Compare the episode with the person's usual pattern and emergency plan. A first seizure, new focal deficit, head injury, pregnancy, fever, severe headache, toxin exposure, or persistent altered mental status calls for prompt assessment. Check capillary glucose and support ordered electrolyte, infection, medication, and brain-injury evaluation. Hypoglycemia, sodium disturbance, alcohol or sedative withdrawal, missed antiseizure medicine, stroke, infection, and other acute illnesses may trigger seizures; treating the convulsion without finding the cause leaves recurrence risk.

During a seizure: protect, time, and support ABCs

Stay with the patient, note the clock, call for help according to the emergency plan, clear nearby hazards, cushion the head, and gently turn the person to the side when feasible to help protect the airway. Assess breathing and oxygenation, and have suction and airway equipment available under protocol. Do not restrain movements, force open the jaw, place an object in the mouth, or offer food, drink, or oral pills until the person is awake and can swallow safely. If the patient is in bed, lower and protect the bed and follow fall precautions. A brief self-limited seizure still needs post-event breathing, injury, and neurologic reassessment.

Activate emergency services or the in-hospital response for a convulsion lasting 5 minutes or more, repeated convulsions without return to baseline, breathing difficulty, major injury, first seizure, or other high-risk context. Do not wait until 30 minutes to identify a dangerous prolonged convulsion. Some patients have a prescribed rescue plan with an earlier action threshold; follow that authorized plan. Document the time each intervention starts and whether movements, awareness, and breathing improve.

Convulsive status epilepticus: parallel rescue and cause search

At about 5 minutes of ongoing generalized convulsion, initiate the status pathway. Support airway, oxygenation, circulation, IV or other access, glucose testing, and preparation for ordered rescue medicine in parallel; the absence of IV access should not create a prolonged delay when an approved alternate route is available. A benzodiazepine is the usual first-line medicine, with agent and route selected by the emergency protocol or individualized plan. Monitor for sedation, hypoventilation, aspiration, and low blood pressure and prepare for assisted ventilation when needed. If seizure activity persists after initial treatment, alert the team promptly rather than repeatedly giving unsupervised doses.

For benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status, the team may use an IV second-line antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate. The ESETT randomized trial found broadly similar effectiveness among these three options; choice depends on contraindications, pregnancy potential, liver and kidney function, interactions, hemodynamics, and local protocol. Verify weight-based orders and infusion monitoring; fosphenytoin requires attention to rhythm and blood pressure, while valproate has important hepatic and reproductive safety considerations. Refractory status may need ICU care, airway control, continuous anesthetic therapy, and EEG-guided assessment under specialist direction. Do not delay first-line rescue while awaiting a complete diagnostic workup.

After movements stop: recovery is an assessment, not an assumption

A postictal period may include sleepiness, confusion, headache, or temporary focal weakness, but the RN must reassess serially rather than label every persistent deficit as postictal. Check airway, oxygenation, vital signs, injury, glucose, temperature, neurologic findings, and time to return toward baseline. Persistent or fluctuating reduced responsiveness after convulsions stop can reflect medication effects, hypoxia, stroke, metabolic illness, or nonconvulsive status epilepticus; the team may order urgent or continuous EEG. Ongoing subtle eye movements, repeated automatisms, or unexplained confusion deserve communication even without obvious shaking. A new focal deficit may also require stroke evaluation.

Longer-term medication and safety teaching

Review the clinician's diagnosis, seizure type, medication regimen, adherence barriers, sleep, alcohol or substance use, interactions, and any individualized rescue medicine. Long-term therapy is selected for the person and seizure type; one medicine does not fit every epilepsy syndrome. Teach patients not to stop antiseizure medication abruptly or change the dose independently. Discuss possible adverse effects and monitoring specific to the prescribed drug, including sedation, mood or behavior changes, rash, liver or blood abnormalities, or drug interactions. Pregnancy planning requires specialist review of seizure control and fetal risk, not abrupt medication withdrawal.

Before discharge, confirm a written seizure action plan: usual event description, when and how a trained person gives rescue treatment, when to call emergency services, and follow-up arrangements. Use teach-back for patient and caregivers. Address bathing and swimming supervision, heights, machinery, and driving according to local law and individualized clinician advice; avoid presenting one driving restriction as universal. Encourage a seizure diary and explain that new prolonged, clustered, or changed events warrant medical contact. Support dignity and privacy: a person recovering from a seizure may be frightened or embarrassed.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Time and describe the event, airway and oxygenation, responsiveness, injury, glucose, medication history, and whether consciousness returns.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate brief self-limited activity from prolonged or repeated convulsions; consider acute triggers and possible nonconvulsive activity when recovery is delayed.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Compromised breathing, convulsive status, recurrent events without recovery, severe metabolic disturbance, and new focal deficit require immediate escalation.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare safe positioning, emergency response, ordered rescue and second-line medicines, airway support, diagnostics, and EEG when indicated.
  5. Take action: Protect without restraining, time the seizure, follow the authorized treatment pathway, monitor adverse effects, and communicate a precise event timeline.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm seizure cessation, stable breathing and perfusion, return toward neurologic baseline, treatment of the trigger, and understanding of the action plan.

Clinical example

A hospitalized adult begins bilateral tonic-clonic movements at 14:02. The RN notes the start time, calls for help, protects the head, clears hazards, supports side positioning when safe, checks breathing, and prepares glucose testing. At 14:07 the convulsion continues, so the team initiates the status protocol and gives ordered rescue medicine while preparing airway support. When movements stop, the client remains unresponsive longer than expected. The RN does not assume the emergency has ended; serial assessment and urgent team review consider medication effects, hypoxia, stroke, and nonconvulsive seizure activity.

Original educational synthesis. Seizure diagnosis, emergency medication choice and dosing, airway management, EEG interpretation, and chronic treatment require current patient data, authorized orders, local protocols, specialist decisions, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official society product.
